GS Delta-One head, Rich Privorotsky, on latest in AI:

Four stories to unpack:
First, CXMT is a legitimate concern for memory economics. 
Second, Microsoft’s Maia 300 custom chips, moving to TSMC’s 2nm process.Incrementally negative for merchant GPU suppliers (NVDA), positive for the custom silicon supply chain and aggregate compute consumption. 
Third, Hock Tan’s comments comparing AI investors to gamblers have been taken wildly out of context. Both Broadcomand Intel reaffirmed exceptionally strong demand for another 2–3 years, potentially through 2030. Tan sees compute demand exceeding supply and explicitly acknowledged that frontier labs generating substantial revenue can afford expensive financing. LT ROI is a legitimate question, but hardly a revelation.  
Fourth, Meta’s Muse Wonder and Wonder Full look genuinely competitive at the frontier,potentially adding another serious player alongside OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Some questions around benchmarking, but impressive nonetheless. Prediction markets also anticipating another major Google release imminently. 

What do I make of all this? Competition fuels competition, and competition requires more compute. The frontier keeps advancing, driven by Western closed source labs trying to outdo one another. Hardly bearish for aggregate compute demand, even if the economics shift around the supply chain. Think the legitimate concerns are around the ability to complete capacity/deliver power relative to expectations and that is fueling further de-rating in the capex vertical.

The annual spread between the S&P 500's earnings yield and the 10Y Note yield is down to -1.5 percentage points, its lowest since 2009.

Since 2022, this yield difference has fallen -440 basis points, its largest 5-year decline since the 1970s.

As a result, the S&P 500's equity risk premium is on track to post its 3rd consecutive negative annual reading, the longest streak since 2002.

This suggests that, on a yield basis, theoretically less risky 10Y Treasuries are now more attractive than the S&P 500.

In other words, investors are receiving a higher yield from Treasuries than from the S&P 500, despite the additional risk of owning stocks.

Historically, a negative equity risk premium has been associated with strong risk appetite and stretched equity valuations.

We expect an eventful Q4 ahead.

The fundamental investment era for crypto

It might be the topic du jour, but I’ve been writing at @RealVision all year that matket forces were correcting years of misalignment and distortion. 

For four years after I entered this space, what vexed me most was how unstable traditional equity-like factors were when applied to this asset class. I wanted to understand what actually drove token value. Quality had to be part of the answer, from first principles, but there weren’t enough protocols with product-market fit, disciplined supply and incentives aligned between insiders and token holders to make the case convincing.

The last cycle left investors disillusioned: too much VC-era grift, dilution and protocol teams whose incentives had little to do with their token holders. Trump’s arrival changed the regulatory environment, while market pressure from pissed off investors and evangelists began to exert pressure. We now have a situation where a protocol cannot just have product-market fit. It must compete on tokenomics / value accrual. Distortions haven't disappeared, but they are declining. Market forces and proper regulatory guardrails will see to that.

The top third of my quality basket is up about 35% through September, while Bitcoin and the cap-weighted Top 100 are both down about 8%. From 2022 through 2025, that basket lost about 71% while Bitcoin gained 88%. Nine months prove little statistically. Still, I’m increasingly convinced that protocols without product-market fit, supply discipline and a credible path for value to reach token holders will underperform those that have all three.
